sm: The hosts open with the weekend FAA grounding of all flights and the questions it raised about air travel security. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said officials were working out whether the cause was user error, an installer error from L3 Harris, or a faulty router. Former FAA official Mark Dumbroft says the reporting points away from a cyber attack and toward failures inside the air traffic infrastructure itself. He describes how the FAA's modernization effort, started in the 1970s as NextGen, never produced a broad integrated upgrade. He notes the system relies on copper wire, replacement parts bought on eBay, and a telecom system about 25 years old. Duffy is asking for about 50 billion dollars, on top of roughly 12 billion Congress already appropriated, and Dumbroft says the money will be well spent if properly overseen. He says a similar glitch could happen again, but layered safety nets, including controllers and pilots, mean the FAA was right to take the conservative approach and no passenger was in danger.

Iranian threats against the president and several cabinet members have led top officials, including Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, to relocate with their families to military bases. Victoria Coates of the Heritage Foundation says Iran tends to hire third-party nationals, often tied to organized crime, rather than use Iranians, and that an FBI cell is working on the threats around the clock. She says Bessent is a target because he has said Iran's economy could contract 25 percent between March 2026 and March 2027, compared with 22 percent over the last three years of the Soviet Union. She calls the drone threats against Trump new and dangerous, and notes that a Wall Street Journal photo of Bessent's house carried location data. On the FAA outage, she says it should prompt an overhaul of aviation systems and closer attention to the contractors involved, along with Nvidia and Microsoft issues. She also says Iran's attacks on Bahrain, home to the Fifth Fleet, are significant, especially with the Theodore Roosevelt carrier group arriving.

DC Bureau Chief Tim Rice describes a Democratic power struggle. In the House, Hakeem Jeffries looks set to become speaker because Democrats won so many seats that little horse trading is needed. In the Senate, there is a push against Chuck Schumer driven by a desire for change after progressives like Abdul El-Sayed and James Talarico won. Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen has launched a challenge with support from Bernie Sanders and many incoming members, while Schumer insists he has the votes. Rice then turns to Nvidia, saying Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnik championed Jensen Huang to Trump and is now criticized for ignoring national security warnings. Bessent and Rubio reportedly worried about advanced chips reaching China. Rice expects Congress to push new AI chip export limits and to question Huang, who has agreed to testify, about trade secrets, possible Chinese spies, and his admitted affairs.
